Approach method

Liquid line − outdoor air, no gauges

The liquid line temperature minus whatever the condenser is rejecting heat into. Lennox prints an approach target on the charging label, but the check works on any equipment — it just needs the right reference and a target, and the buttons below cover both. Its advantage: temperatures only, so the charge can be checked without hooking up gauges and losing refrigerant every visit.

Lennox charging labels give the approach target for that model — often a single number per size, held to ±1 °F, so tighten the tolerance above when you're working to a real label. Read it off the unit in front of you rather than carrying one over from the last job.

Any brand, in cooling: the target is the condenser's design split minus the subcool the maker already specs. Approach = split − subcool, so if the condenser rejects heat the way it was designed to, the two targets are the same target.

Target approach = design split (20 °F) − target subcool (10 °F)

Design split comes from the equipment's efficiency: more condenser surface rejects the same heat at a smaller temperature difference. It's an estimate, so keep the tolerance at ±3 or wider, and confirm the first reading against subcool with gauges on.

The most accurate target on any equipment: record the approach once, with the charge known good, and compare against it from then on. A benchmark is only valid near the conditions it was taken at — this flags a reading if the reference temperature has moved more than 10 °F.

Measured approach
—
Target
—
Condenser split
—
Approach = liquid line temp − outdoor air temp

Take the outdoor air in the shade at the coil inlet, not downwind of the fan. Approach rises as the charge falls, so a high reading is usually low charge — but a dirty condenser coil, a slow fan or recirculating hot air raise it too, which is what the condenser split is there to tell you apart.

Charge by weight on a new install, a line-set change or after a recovery — on every brand. Approach is for checking and trimming an existing charge, and it wants a system that has run 15 minutes on high stage with a clean filter and a clean condenser.

Cooling mode, running at least 15 minutes with the doors closed. Measure in the return close to the unit and in the supply plenum just past the coil (out of sight of any heat strips).

A screening test, not a replacement for measuring airflow. Check the refrigerant charge and the blower setting together — low charge also shrinks the split.

Total external static pressure

Blower running on the cooling (high) speed, filter in place, every panel and door closed, all registers open. Drill or use the test ports: the return reading goes between the return duct and the blower (ahead of the filter), the supply reading in the supply plenum past the coil. Enter both as plain positive numbers — the return reading is negative on the manometer and this adds the magnitudes.

Total external static pressure
—
Return side
—
Supply side
—
Of the rating
—
TESP = |return static| + |supply static|

Where the pressure is going (optional)

Drop across a single component: one reading on each side of it, entered as the difference. These are not part of TESP — they tell you which part is doing the choking.

Most residential blowers are rated for 0.5 in. w.c. total external static; some high-static ECM equipment is rated 0.8–1.0. The rating and the matching blower table are in the installation manual — once TESP is known, that table gives the actual CFM the blower is moving.

Clocking the gas meter

Every other gas appliance off firstWater heater, dryer, range, fireplace, second furnace — and any standing pilot. Anything else drawing gas during the timing makes the furnace read overfired. Turn the furnace to high fire (two-stage) and let it run a few minutes before timing.

The small test dial on the meter face, not the odometer-style register. Pick the smallest one that still takes 15 seconds or more to come around.

Measured firing rate
—
Gas flow
—
Target input
—
Of target
—
Input BTU/h = (3600 ÷ seconds) × revolutions × dial size (ft³) × heating value (BTU/ft³)

1030 BTU/ft³ is a common default for natural gas; the local utility publishes the real number and it moves with the season. Propane is metered by the gallon, so clocking does not apply — set propane by manifold pressure and orifice size instead.

Furnace temperature rise

Let it run 10–15 minutes on high fire with a clean filter and every register open. Measure in the return close to the furnace and in the supply plenum out of line of sight of the heat exchanger, or the radiant heat reads high.

Blower airflow

Measured rise
—
Output

Input used
—
CFM = output BTU/h ÷ (1.08 × rise) (1.08 corrected for altitude)

The input comes from the clocked rate when the meter has been clocked, otherwise from the nameplate on the Clock the Meter screen. Rise above the nameplate range means too little air (or too much gas); below it means too much air (or too little gas) — clock the meter before touching the blower speed.

Indoor vs outdoor

Enthalpy difference
—
Moisture difference
—

Enthalpy is total heat (sensible + latent). The moisture difference is the water the system has to deal with in any outside air that gets in.

Sends indoor wet bulb & outdoor dry bulb straight into the SH/SC tab's piston superheat target.

What these mean
  • Relative humidity — how full the air is of water compared with the most it could hold at that temperature. Same water, colder air = higher RH.
  • Moisture (humidity ratio) — the actual water in the air, in grains per pound of dry air (7,000 grains = 1 lb). It doesn't change when air is only heated or cooled.
  • Absolute humidity — water per cubic foot of air (gr/ft³), the weight of water in a given space.
  • Moisture capacity — the most water the air can hold at its temperature before it condenses (100% RH). Warm air holds far more than cool air — why a cold coil wrings water out.
  • Dew point — cool the air to this and water starts condensing. A coil (or duct) colder than the dew point gets wet.
  • Wet bulb — what a wetted thermometer reads; used for piston charging targets and capacity. Enthalpy — total heat per pound of air.
  • On the chart: left-to-right is dry bulb, up is moisture. Curved lines are % RH (the top one is saturation); dashed diagonal lines are wet bulb. Heating or cooling without adding/removing water moves a point straight sideways.
ASHRAE psychrometric equations (Hyland–Wexler saturation pressure), corrected for altitude.

Pressures in psig. Values below 0 psig shown in inHg vacuum. Blends: use bubble (liquid) for subcool, dew (vapor) for superheat.

Plot a system

Cycle results

Reading a P-h chart
  • Up is pressure (absolute, log scale). Right is enthalpy — heat content in Btu per pound of refrigerant.
  • The dome: left edge = saturated liquid, right edge = saturated vapor, top = critical point. Left of the dome is subcooled liquid, inside is boiling/condensing liquid + vapor, right is superheated vapor.
  • 1 → 2 compressor (adds the heat of compression) · 2 → 3 condenser (desuperheat, condense, subcool) · 3 → 4 metering device (straight down: no heat added, some liquid flashes) · 4 → 1 evaporator (picks up the refrigeration effect).
  • Temperature lines run straight up in the liquid, flat across the dome (sloped for blends with glide) and curve down in the vapor. Quality lines show % vapor; entropy lines show ideal compression.
  • Enthalpy uses the ASHRAE reference (0 Btu/lb for saturated liquid at −40°F), like most English-unit charts. Charts with another reference show different numbers, but the differences (refrigeration effect, heat of compression) are the same.

🚨 Emergencies

  • Smell gas: no switches, phones or flames inside. Get everyone out, shut the gas at the meter if safe, call the gas utility / 911 from outside.
  • CO 70 ppm or more: everyone out and call 911. 36–69 ppm: ventilate and shut off sources. 9–35 ppm: tell the customer and ventilate.
  • Electric shock: don't touch the person until the power is off. Call 911; start CPR / use an AED if trained.
  • Refrigerant on skin or eyes: get to fresh air; warm (not hot) water on skin — don't rub; flush eyes 15 minutes; get medical help.
  • Heat stroke (confusion, hot dry skin, collapse): call 911 and cool them down right away.
  • Burns: cool running water for 10+ minutes; get help for large or deep burns.

Evaporator TD

TD = box air temperature − saturated suction temperature. Measure with the box near setpoint and the coil clear of frost.

Blends use the dew point. R-448A and R-449A glide about 8–10 °F, and some unit cooler makers rate TD on the midpoint (about 4–5 °F below dew), which reads a larger TD. The unit cooler's rated TD comes first; high-humidity boxes (produce, meat) run lower TDs.

Freeze-cycle check

Look up the expected freeze time on the machine's chart for today's air and water temperatures, then time a full freeze and harvest.
